q: How do I guard the other team's best player without fouling out?
a: First job is pattern recognition of their bag — watch the moves, watch the repetition, and you'll know exactly when to strike. Start with ball denial: work out who the ball gets the most output from and stop that person connecting with it. If they do get it, pressure — but the right way. Reaching in constantly won't work; one missed swipe and he drives straight by you. Patience is the preferred method. Defence is an art — become your own artist.

q: I'd rather work on my scoring — why does defence matter so much?
a: Because defence fuels offense. A defensive stop gives you and your team two moves on the chess board instead of one — you got the stop, and now you've earned another chance to make the board harder for your opponent. On defence, focus on learning the art of being in the right place at the right time; even the tiniest millisecond makes a difference. The by-product of great defence is a flowing offense. The game is like chess — possession by possession, it can be altered to reach your team's goals.

q: How do I get better at reading plays before they happen on defence?
a: Pattern recognition — understanding the situation at hand and, based on history, the potential outcome. Example: you're defending a 2-on-1 fast break and you know the ball handler hates passing it up. Commit to the trailer without the ball, make the ball handler THINK you've committed to them, then switch back to make their shot harder. Prepping for basketball isn't just physical, it's mental — go into your games prepped mentally on defence and usually everything flows and feels locked in. When you proactively think ahead, you're always one step ahead of your opponents.

q: Everyone on my team wants to be the scorer. How do I actually stand out?
a: Here's the truth most players avoid: your weaknesses are louder than your strengths. Everybody wants the ball in late-game moments — very few build their identity around what the team needs. If you can't guard your position, you're a liability. If you can't rotate, you break the system. If you can't make the extra pass, you stall progress. Basketball is not about highlights, it's about habits — become the player your team needs and you'll never be off the floor.

q: My coach says I need better basketball IQ. What does that actually mean?
a: IQ isn't talent. IQ is fast pattern recognition built through reps — the more situations you've seen and played through, the quicker you read the next one. Same deal with defence: it isn't effort, it's discipline under fatigue. Neither one is a gift you're born with; both get built. Stop chasing highlights and start stacking habits.

q: How do I work out what I really need to improve this season?
a: Ask your teammates where you're a liability. Not your friends — your teammates. If their answer makes you uncomfortable… good. That's where development starts. You don't grow from compliments, you grow from clarity. Accountability equals progress.

q: When I grab an offensive rebound and can't score, what's the right play?
a: If you can't go straight back up for the bucket — RESET. Here's the part most players don't get: a reset frustrates your opponent because now they have to commit to another 14 seconds of defence. Run a team through multiple possessions of beautiful passing and floor spacing and you're wearing them out pass by pass, rotation by rotation. A reset gives you more options that lead to a bucket — and leaves the other team depleted from constantly covering and rotating.

q: My threes aren't falling in games — how do I get better looks?
a: First check the teams you're on: are they MOVING the ball? This generation wants the three but thinks it's a higher percentage taken alone — no, no, no. When the ball moves multiple times in one possession, whatever defence is being played will usually show a crack, and that's when you attack. Straight-to-the-point passing will always lead to a good shot — it doesn't have to be fancy. And the by-product created while you're passing? Chemistry. The game is simple; we complicate it.

q: I'm not a scorer or flashy. Is defence enough to build my game on?
a: Everything starts with defence. Not scoring, not talent, not being flashy — defence. It's discipline when you're tired, communication when it's uncomfortable, holding your position when things get chaotic. Anyone can attack; not everyone can protect. Build your game on protecting and there will always be a spot on the floor for you.

q: How do I find confidence on court when my shot isn't falling?
a: Defence gives you confidence. Whenever you get a steal, a block, or force a change of possession — at that exact moment, harness the energy from that stop and let it carry into your next move to shift the game in your favour. Basketball is small real estate, so a stop is an instant momentum swing; in footy it takes a hundred metres, on a court it happens NOW. Use your defence to motivate your team too — get everyone on that defensive mindset and the easy pickings come.

q: How do I use my game footage to actually improve, not just make highlight clips?
a: Watching yourself back requires a certain amount of humility. You're not watching for highlights or clout — you're watching for SELF-IMPROVEMENT and critiquing. Understanding your weaknesses and areas of opportunity through footage is an undervalued skill: we all have access, but do we have intent? And remember, it's a full 40-minute game — not one highlight or one move. It's a chess game that plays out till the last buzzer, so watch it that way.

q: My coach teaches me things at training but I never get to try them in real games.
a: Find yourself a free-flowing run — that's where you practice whatever you learn from your coaches in a non-judgmental, progressive environment. It gives you the chance to make mistakes and get feedback on the spot — connecting then correcting is an amazing way to RETAIN information. Not clout basketball. Purposeful basketball. Play with purpose, Youngblood.

q: Pickup at my courts always turns into arguments over foul calls — what's the go?
a: Here's the truth: pick-up runs are all about accountability, because there is no ref — YOU are the ref. That unwritten responsibility means you keep your integrity at all times and just speak the truth. You fouled someone and they call it? Honour it. It's casual pickup, my guy. If you want to argue calls, go play organised basketball — simple facts. Respect the game that gave you life.

q: What should I say to a teammate who keeps missing shots?
a: Careful with the empty 'good shot' when it was a bad shot — keep it productive, not pessimistic, and not fake either. Your words could literally be the difference between an L and a W. Team morale and chemistry are vital, no matter how much skill you stack on one team. So say something they can use: next one, adjust, let's push on defence. That's how the whole team leaves the house and comes home with a W mindset.

q: A guy at our run plays and reacts differently and the boys get frustrated. What should we do?
a: I'm not a professional, but supporting my daughter since her diagnosis taught me to look at this differently. Be mindful that some people may not RECEIVE your communication well or understand what you mean. If something about the way someone plays or conducts themselves seems plainly obvious to you, ask yourself: maybe they just need a bit more patience and calm. Autism is severely misunderstood in the sports world — I've had to step in on court when guys were having a go at someone with no idea they were on the spectrum. So when you run: be considerate, be kind.

q: My best mate and I are trying out for the same spot — should I stop helping him?
a: Collaboration beats competition. Competition is a battle where only one really wins and the rest miss out. Collaboration creates opportunity for everyone to eat and enjoy what's being served at the table. Keep helping your mate, push each other hard, and you both walk into that tryout better players. Do things with the intention to benefit others and it goes far and wide — you're planting a seed that grows for generations.

q: Everyone says foul baiting is smart because it gets free throws — should I be doing it?
a: Real talk: stop. Just stop. Foul baiting might buy you a whistle, but it ruins the game for everyone on that court — including you. Play the right way and get your buckets through real work. Don't ruin the game we love.

q: My mates all drink Prime before games — should I be drinking it too?
a: Here's the truth: you don't need a crazy diet, you just need smarter choices. Prime? No thanks — coconut water instead. Two natural ingredients versus seventeen made-up ones. That's the simple test for a lot of this stuff: fewer, more natural ingredients usually wins. And with any supplement or fancy drink — especially while you're still growing — run it past your GP or an Accredited Sports Dietitian first. I'm sharing what works for me, not writing you a plan.

q: I'm a teenager — will learning to cook actually help my basketball?
a: Real talk: if you want to improve your game on the court, learn how to cook. Everyone yells 'cook him' — well, to reach chef status, start by cooking literally. A recipe is like a play: understand the steps, execute them in order, adjust when something doesn't go to plan. Making your own food builds discipline away from the court — when you understand what fuels your body, you can train harder, recover better and take more responsibility for your game. It won't replace practice, but it builds the mindset and patience that show up on the hardwood.

q: How do I eat healthy without everything tasting bland and boring?
a: Eating clean is easy — we make it hard. Healthy doesn't have to mean bland. If you feel like a dish, don't order it, don't go to a restaurant — CREATE it. Every culture has dishes that cater for your health; a korma done right is tasty as, with the benefits to back it. Learn to cook the food you actually crave and the healthy part takes care of itself.

q: Why do I have good games and bad games even though I train the same?
a: Ask yourself what you're doing OUTSIDE the game — because that's usually the answer. It's lack of consistency in some areas: what you do away from basketball will affect your craft. 2am sleeper, 7am up for school or work? You've already lost the day before you touched a ball. Nutrition and self-care are vital to performing at your peak, and here's the good news — you don't need a crazy diet, you just need smarter choices. Looking after yourself is the key to performing consistently in every area.

q: Do I need a massive breakfast to set up a big day of basketball?
a: We get fooled into thinking breakfast needs to be huge. Sometimes it's four ingredients done well. Try one small tweak — a new flavour in your eggs changes the whole meal. Same as your game on the court: every possession can be adjusted, and every adjustment counts, no matter how small.

q: I rush everything when the game speeds up and make silly mistakes. How do I slow down?
a: Train it off the court first. Every time you catch yourself rushing through your day, slow down and tell yourself: nothing is chasing me, no need to rush. Mindset is a lifestyle, not a game-day switch. On the court it becomes this — slow your mind down, speed your body up. Master that art and the game gets slower even when you're outrunning everyone.

q: When my shot's not falling early, my whole game falls apart. Help?
a: It starts with your inner thought before you even leave the house: 'whatever has passed I can't control.' Then work the ladder. First warm-up three misses — 'I will make the next one.' A few more in a row — 'I need to adjust.' Misses stacking up IN the game — 'I will push harder on defence.' Real talk: the buckets become easier after that.

q: One bad play and my whole game unravels. How do I reset mid-game?
a: Positive mindset, possession by possession — that's what unlocks flow state. Ask yourself: are you remembering the last game, the last mistake, and basing your next performance on the past? Wrong mindset. The play is gone; the only possession that exists is the one in front of you. Reset, lock in on the next stop, and let the flow come back.

q: My confidence is gone and my self-talk is brutal. How do I turn it around?
a: I'll be straight with you — confidence was a struggle for me until not long ago. Self-doubt, negative self-talk, low self-esteem, all of it, and you keep going but not at your full potential. Two things changed it for me: what I said to myself, and who I kept around me. Talk your talk, talk your truth, tell yourself you've got this. And surround yourself with positive people who just want to enjoy the moment for what it is — not compete to the point it turns toxic. Let the good vibes roll in. And real talk — if the brutal self-talk hangs around no matter what you do, don't carry it solo: talking to someone you trust, or a psychologist, is a strong move, not a weak one.

q: Some days raising my autistic child feels impossible. How do you keep going?
a: I'm not a professional — this is just what raising my non-verbal daughter taught me. Was it hard? Hell yeah. It's unpredictable: one day everything's perfect, the next you're getting the call from school to come pick her up. But those moments compound over the years, and you accept that this is YOUR way of life — and it's beautiful, even when it's misunderstood. In return I gained a skill I now use everywhere: patience and understanding of the situation at hand. The process is beautiful — believe in it, and on the rough days lean on people you trust, because you don't have to carry it alone. And if you ever feel qualified support is needed — for her or for you — go get it, I'll always say that.

q: My son leaves the court frustrated after bad games. Do I correct him, encourage him or give space?
a: I'm not a professional and I'm not here to tell anyone how to parent — this is lived experience from years watching local basketball up close. Before you pick correct, encourage or space, look beneath the behaviour and ask what he might actually be experiencing in that moment. The real story is in the habits, the body language, the responses to mistakes and pressure — not the scoreboard. Over time you see what helps a young person grow and what pushes them further away. Start by understanding the person behind the performance.

q: My daughter isn't developing as fast as her basketball teammates. Should I be worried?
a: Every child has potential, but not every child follows the same path. The goal was never to manufacture identical players — it's to understand them, nurture them and help each one find the lane where they can grow. Different ages, different bodies, different routines, different starting points. Watch her habits and how she responds over time, not the comparison to the girl next to her. And if you ever feel qualified support is needed, go get it — I'll always say that.

q: My parents and coach both have big plans for me. Whose dream am I chasing?
a: Here's the truth: the goal is YOUR full potential. Not your parents', not your coach's, not your bro's — YOURS. The people around you can back the journey, but the reps are yours to do and the love for the game has to be yours too. And unlocking that potential isn't an overnight drug — it's rep by rep, breath by breath. If the weight of everyone's plans is getting heavy, say it out loud to someone you trust — that conversation is part of the work too.

q: School and life are stressing me out — is it bad that basketball is my escape?
a: Real talk: basketball for a lot of us is about escaping the noise. We block it out by balling — we laugh, we compete, we fight for possession, we talk deep and meaningful, and most importantly we love the game that keeps us sane. That's not a bad thing, that's one of the game's greatest gifts. Just make sure the court isn't the only place you deal with the heavy stuff — if the noise is getting loud, talk to someone you trust off the court too.

q: I'm nervous to rock up to pickup runs alone without my mates.
a: Go anyway, Youngblood. Don't wait for a run to get organised — get out there and put yourself in those runs whether your friends are there or not. Pick-up is one of the best ways to learn the game: more reps, more effort, more growth. And you'll meet good people out there — that's the beauty of the sport.

q: I work full-time and barely train. Does my life off the court count for anything?
a: Anyone 35-plus still playing will tell you: whatever profession you fell in love with and perfected shows up in your game. My years teaching at Samsung taught me confidence, perseverance, empathy — and those exact things are what make it easy to connect with everyone on the court. People won't remember every play; they remember how YOU made them FEEL. So don't write off the day job. The skills you're building there travel with you onto the hardwood.

q: I give up on new things when I'm bad at them straight away — any advice?
a: That ugly start IS the good part. The beauty of starting a process is making mistakes, learning from them, adjusting, adapting — then enjoying the final result. That's how you level up. Your first meal or your first jump shot won't be perfect. You improve by doing it again.

q: Do pre-game routines actually matter or is it all just superstition?
a: They matter more than most people think. How you conduct yourself before, during and even after the game affects your next game — and all the ones after that. Consistency is key here, and one of the best doing it consistently is SGA from the OKC Thunder — definitely a player whose routines and habits off the court are worth following. Build yours, then repeat it.

q: My left hand is useless and defenders just force me left every time. How do I fix it?
a: Real talk: your weak hand doesn't get fixed in games, it gets fixed in boring reps nobody claps for. For the next month, open every session with ten minutes of left-hand-only work — pound dribbles standing still, then walking, then attacking a chair and finishing left off the proper footwork. Take it off the court too: brush your teeth lefty, open doors lefty, carry the shopping in lefty — you're teaching your brain that hand exists. Then in games, go left on purpose early, in the low-stakes minutes, so it holds up later when it matters. It's going to feel ugly for two or three weeks and that's the exact window where most players quit on it. Push through and the ugly turns into a weapon, because a guard who can genuinely go both ways is twice as hard to scout. Reps over highlights, my guy.

q: I keep turning the ball over three or four times a game. How do I clean it up?
a: Here's the truth: not all turnovers are the same mistake, so first work out which ones are yours. Most come down to three things — passing to a spot instead of a person, dribbling into a crowd with no plan, or playing faster than you can think. Next game, count them honestly, and afterwards write down what each one actually was, because a pattern you can name is a pattern you can train. If it's crowds, drill your jump stop and pivot so you always have an out; if it's picked-off passes, practise the fake — fake low, throw high, and never lob it lazily across the court. Then slow the mind down: catch, see the whole floor for one beat, then decide. What you don't do is go timid and stop making plays, because a scared pass is still a bad pass. Cleaner decisions, same courage.

q: The guy I have to guard is way quicker than me. How do I not get cooked?
a: You don't beat speed with speed — you beat it with angles and brains, like chess against a faster clock. Give him half a step of cushion so his first burst doesn't beat you, and never lunge or reach, because the moment you lunge you're watching his back. Spend the first quarter scouting him: which hand does he love, does he actually pull up or does he only want the rim? Then take away his best move — force him to the weak hand, use the sideline as your second defender, and if he's no shooter, sag off and dare the jumper. Get help organised too: talk early, so your mates know you're funnelling him somewhere on purpose. Quick players feed on open floor and panic; make him play in traffic at your pace and he's suddenly ordinary. Defence is decisions before it's feet.

q: I always get matched up on players way taller and stronger. What actually works?
a: Rule one: never play their game. No wrestling in the post, no shots up through their chest — that's donating the ball. Your weapons are space and pace, so attack before their defence is set, and use change of speed: slow him to sleep, then go, and go opposite to where you moved him. Live on floaters and angled finishes off the glass — the floater exists exactly because of long arms — and finish off two feet so you can absorb the bump. Drag him away from the ring with ball screens and movement, because big and strong hates guarding in open space. On the boards, don't out-jump him, out-position him: hit his body early and be first to the spot. Thirty years of ball taught me the smaller player wins with a plan, not with pride.

q: My coach switches between zone and man and I get completely lost. Help me understand defence?
a: One question sorts out ninety percent of it: am I guarding a person or protecting a space? In man, you own your player — ball, you, your man in a triangle, and you move every time either one does. In zone, you own an area, and your eyes live on the ball: when it comes into your patch you close out hard, when it leaves you sink back and talk. There's one rule that saves you in both: always see the ball. And if you ever genuinely lose the plot mid-play, sprint to the paint and find work from there — protecting the ring is never the wrong answer. After training, ask your coach to walk you through it on the whiteboard; that question doesn't make you look dumb, it makes you look switched on. Then talk on court — calling out what you see organises your own brain as much as your teammates'.

q: When teams full-court press us I panic and throw the ball away. Help?
a: Real talk: a press isn't built to steal the ball, it's built to steal your calm — the turnovers follow the panic. So beat it by slowing your mind while your body stays sharp. Before the inbound, one breath, and know where your two outlets are. Then the non-negotiables: meet every pass instead of waiting for it, never dribble into the corner or the sideline trap, and never pick up your dribble without knowing where the pass is going. The middle of the floor kills a press, so someone must always flash to the middle — be that someone. If you do get trapped, pivot strong, fake, and find the reversal pass; the trap always leaves someone free behind it. And flip the story: a broken press is a layup at the other end, so start seeing pressure as free points coming, not danger.

q: Free throws with the game on the line turn my legs to jelly. What do the calm players know?
a: They know one thing: the routine shoots the free throw, not the moment. Build one now and make it sacred — same dribbles, same breath, same eyes on your spot, every single free throw you ever shoot, including the lazy ones at training. That way, when the gym is loud and your heart is going, your body just runs the program it's run a thousand times. At the line, make the breath out longer than the breath in — a long slow exhale genuinely settles the body. Aim small: pick the back of the rim, not the whole ring. And reframe the shakes — nerves mean the moment matters, and you don't need them gone, you just need your routine louder than they are. If you miss, you're the same player you were before the whistle; the ones who want that line are simply the ones who've shot thousands alone.

q: Down one, last possession — do I take the shot or give it up? I froze last week.
a: You froze because you made it about you — hero or villain, and your brain didn't like either. Here's the fix: the last possession is just another possession, and the right answer is always the same one — take what the defence gives. If you're open or you've got the matchup you want, shoot it with no apology. If two defenders come at you, the pass is the winning play, full stop — the great ones want the moment but never force it. Decide before the ball is even live: if they switch I do this, if they trap I hit that man. Run whatever your coach called first, obviously. Then live with the result, because missed game-winners are the tax every willing player pays, and being willing is the whole game.

q: I only get on court when the game is already decided. Is garbage time even worth anything?
a: Here's the truth: garbage time is an audition, and most kids waste it chucking hero shots to pad the memory. Coaches watch those minutes closely, because that's where they see who you are when nothing is handed to you. So treat your four minutes like a grand final: sprint the floor, talk on defence, box out every time, and run the offence properly — running the actual plays in a blowout tells the coach you can be trusted with real minutes. Chase effort stats: a deflection, a charge, an offensive board. When you're on the bench, be the loudest teammate in the gym — coaches clock the sulkers and they clock the ones up at every huddle. Then, away from game day, ask your coach privately what you need to show to earn more time. Minutes are earned inside the minutes you're given.

q: Bad ref calls cost us on the weekend and I completely lost my head. How do I deal?
a: Hard truth first: you will never play a season with perfect refereeing, so a player who tilts at calls is handing away games for free. Most refs at our level are volunteers doing their best at full speed — respect the game includes respecting the whistle. The seconds after a bad call are a test, and the test is next-play speed: one breath, say 'next play' to yourself, sprint back. The player arguing is a player out of the play, which means for those seconds your team is four on five. If the calls keep coming, that's information, not injustice — the refs are calling it tight today, so stop reaching and move your feet. Let your captain or coach have the calm conversation with officials; that's their job, not yours. Your job is the scoreboard, and the scoreboard doesn't hear complaints.

q: I get thirty minutes and a ring to myself. What should I actually do with it?
a: Structure beats vibes every time, so here's a session worth stealing. Five minutes of ballhandling to warm up — stationary series or two-ball, at game speed, not casual. Ten minutes of finishing: pick five spots each side and run a layup package — regular, reverse, floater — off a self-pass, both hands, off the proper foot. Ten minutes of shooting off movement: catch and shoot from a spot, chase your own rebound, sprint to the next spot, and count your makes — chase a number like fifty and write it in your phone. Last five minutes, free throws on tired legs with your full routine, because that's when they count in games. Two rules over the top: every rep at game speed, and log your numbers so you can watch yourself climb. The same session twice a week beats a random two-hour mess every time.

q: I don't have a team right now and train alone. How do I stay sharp and motivated?
a: A solo season can be your best season if you treat it like a program instead of a mood. Write the week down — three sessions, what each one covers, and a number attached to every drill, because numbers are your teammate now: they give you something to beat when nobody's watching. Film yourself on your phone once a week; the camera is the most honest coach you'll ever have and it's free. Then find one live run — lunchtime pickup, a social comp, anything with real bodies once a week — because reads and decisions only sharpen against humans. Give the whole thing a finish line: a tryout date, a season start, something you're building toward, so the work has a direction. Habits over highlights — alone is where you build the stuff that shows up loud when you're back on a team.

q: How do I watch NBA and NBL games so I'm actually learning, not just vibing?
a: Pick one player who plays your position and watch only them for a full quarter — especially when they don't have the ball. The broadcast follows the ball, but the learning lives away from it: watch their feet, their spacing, the angle they set screens, where they stand on defence, how much they talk. Pause and predict — before the pass happens, guess where it's going, then see if you were right; that's pattern recognition training, and basketball is chess played at a sprint. Rewind one action three times instead of watching three games once. Then steal exactly one thing per game — a cut, a footwork move, a way of sealing a defender — and take it to your very next session so it doesn't stay trivia. A quarter studied properly beats a whole night of highlights consumed.

q: I train heaps but I've stopped improving. What's going on?
a: Plateaus usually mean comfortable reps — you're rehearsing what you're already good at, and your body has stopped needing to adapt. Audit one honest week: how many minutes were genuinely hard, where you were failing and adjusting? If you never miss and never fail in training, you're maintaining, not building. So change one dial at a time: speed (every drill with a clock or a defender), constraint (left hand only, two-dribble limit), or competition (find runs where you're the worst player in the gym — that's the best room to be in). Measure monthly, not daily, because growth is stairs, not a ramp: flat, flat, flat, jump — and the flat bit is where most people quit, right before the jump. One more thing players hate hearing: rest is training too, because tired reps teach tired habits. Be patient with results and stubborn with the process.

q: I'm good for three quarters, then my legs die in the fourth. How do I build a bigger tank?
a: Skill sessions at cruise pace don't build a fourth quarter — you have to train the engine on purpose, and train it basketball-shaped. Twice a week, end your session with hard intervals that copy the game: sideline-to-sideline seventeens, or full-court attack-the-ring then sprint back, with work-and-rest gaps like real ball, not a long jog that trains nothing you use. Then here's the bit most players skip: practise skill tired. Put your free throws and finishing at the end of the session when your legs are gone, because the fourth quarter is played on exactly those legs. In games, spend energy like money — sprint when it matters, steal rest at dead balls and free throws, stop gambling for steals that cost you a chase-back. Give it four to six weeks of honest work before you judge it. Fourth quarters aren't found on game day; they're built on the days nobody sees.

q: Our best player never passes, even when I'm wide open. What can I actually do?
a: First, don't sulk your way to the corner, because a flat, invisible teammate is even easier to ignore. Get open where he can't miss you: cut hard to the ring the moment his drive dies, slide to the spot his eyes go when he's in trouble, and crash the offensive glass — real talk, you'll touch the ball more off his misses than his passes. Then talk to him like a teammate, not a prosecutor: 'when you drive baseline I'll be at the forty-five — hit me and I'll hit you back next play.' When the pass finally comes, reward it loudly — hype him up, make passing to you feel like a highlight. If it's genuinely costing the team, that's a conversation for the coach, raised privately and framed about the team, not about him. And whatever you do, don't become him out of spite — be the player everyone wants to run with.

q: I just joined a new club where everyone's been mates for years. How do I fit in?
a: Earn belonging with actions before words — new-team trust is built, not talked into existence. For the first month: be early, help carry gear, and learn every single name fast, because names matter more than people realise. On court, be the connector — talk on defence, celebrate teammates' buckets louder than your own, make the extra pass; nobody freezes out the player who makes them look good. Off court, don't force it or audition for the friend group with jokes — consistent beats impressive, every time. Find one teammate to get shots up with before training; one genuine connection is the doorway to the whole group. Give it six honest weeks of showing up before you judge whether you fit. Mate, every tight group you've ever envied started with someone being the new guy.

q: I want to be captain next season. How do I actually earn it?
a: Here's the truth: captaincy is recognised, not requested — coaches don't hand the armband to whoever wants it, they hand it to whoever's already doing the job. So start doing it now. Be the standard at training: first in every drill, sprinting when the team is flat, zero shortcuts when nobody's watching. Lead the players nobody else lifts — the new kid, the benched kid — because hyping the stars is easy and lifting the bottom of the roster is leadership. Own your mistakes out loud: 'my fault, I've got it' — teams follow that voice like nothing else. Then tell your coach straight: 'I want to help lead this group — what do you need from me?' That conversation alone is a captain's move. And if someone else gets the title anyway, keep leading exactly the same, because titles rotate and standards don't.

q: I've been benched the last few games and my coach hasn't said why. What now?
a: Don't guess and stew, because the stories you invent at eleven at night are nearly always worse and wronger than the truth. Ask properly: pick a calm moment after training — never straight after a game — and ask one question: 'what do I need to work on to earn more minutes?' That question tells a coach you're coachable, and honestly, it changes some players' minutes on its own. Then listen without defending yourself, even if the answer stings; write it down when you get home. Spend the next two weeks attacking exactly that thing at training, visibly, so the change is impossible to miss. Meanwhile, be the best bench player in the gym — up at every huddle, loud for your teammates — because coaches notice sulkers and they notice sprinters. A benching is a chapter, not a verdict, and how you carry it is part of the tryout.

q: I coach under-12s and one boy sulks every time I sub him off. Any advice, coach to coach?
a: From watching a lot of local junior ball: the sulk is almost never about the sub, it's about the story the kid tells himself — subbed off means coach hates me, means I failed. So beat the story with information before you deal with the emotion. Early in the season, tell the whole squad how your rotations work — everyone sits, it's rest and learning, not punishment — so a sub carries no verdict. When you take him off, give him one line: 'breather, you're back in five' or 'watch how their five sets screens and tell me at the break'. That second one is gold — a bench job turns exile into an assignment. Then praise the behaviour you want the moment you see it: 'loved how you came off today, that's a teammate'. A quiet word with his parents helps too, so the car ride home tells the same story you do. Give it a few weeks — some kids need the pattern proven before they trust it.

q: I airballed in front of everyone and now I don't want to shoot. How do I get past it?
a: Youngblood, everyone who's ever really played has thrown one — thirty years of ball, I've seen gyms full of airballs and the game just keeps moving. Here's the truth: nobody is replaying your miss, because they're all too busy replaying their own stuff. The danger was never the airball, it's the story you write after it — 'I'm not a shooter' — because that sentence kills a hundred future shots. So give the miss a funeral: next solo session, shoot that exact shot twenty-five times, count your makes, then it's buried and done. In your next game, the first open look you get, shoot it — passing up open shots teaches your brain the fear was right, and you can't afford that lesson. Last thing: learn to grin at it. The player who can laugh at his own airball is bulletproof, and the game respects a short memory.

q: My daughter's team loses by thirty every week and she's losing heart. How do I help?
a: Real talk for you first: development and ladder position are not the same thing, and some of the most improved kids I've watched came out of losing teams — they got the hardest matchups and the most minutes while the stacked teams' kids watched. Your job is to shift the scoreboard at home. Before each game, help her pick two targets she fully controls — box out every rebound, three deflections, talk on every defensive play — and if she wins those, the day was a win, whatever the scoreboard says. In the car afterwards, ask 'what did you win today?' before anyone mentions the score. Watch her effort across the season, because effort that survives losing is the exact muscle that carries people through life, and tell her you see it. If she's flat for a night, that's sport; if she's miserable for weeks on end, that's a bigger conversation about whether this team is still the right fit for her. Losing seasons can build players that winning streaks never could — but only if the adults around them frame it right.

q: I got cut at rep tryouts and I'm gutted. What should I do now?
a: Getting cut hurts because you care — there's nothing broken about you for feeling it, so take the first couple of days to be filthy about it. Then trade the mystery for information: ask the coach, politely, for the two main things that kept you out. Most coaches will tell you, and now you've got a program instead of a wound. Next: keep playing games somewhere — domestic, school, social — because the kid who gets cut and plays a full season of real minutes often comes back past the kid who made it and sat on a bench. Attack those two things all season and track the work so you can see it stack. Remember what a cut actually is: one selector's opinion on one weekend, and plenty of seriously good players at every level have one in their story. I can't promise you next year's list — nobody honest can — but I can promise the players who respond like this give themselves a real crack at it.

q: How does the rep basketball pathway actually work in Australia, and how do I get noticed?
a: Rough map, mate: domestic club ball at your local association is the base, rep teams sit above that at the same association, and state programs and state teams sit above rep — with school ball running alongside the whole way, feeding the same pool. Practically: play strong domestic minutes, then front up to your association's rep tryouts — dates live on the association's website and socials, so set a reminder now, because missing registration is the most common own-goal going. On getting noticed: junior selectors watch defence, running the floor, and coachability harder than they watch scoring, because every gym in the country is full of scorers — so talk on defence, sprint every change of possession, and visibly listen when a coach speaks. Ask your current coach for the honest read on where you sit and what to build this season; they often know the selectors' language better than you do. And hold this: the pathway isn't one door. School, domestic and rep all feed each other, late developers push through every single year, and the players who keep stacking seasons are the ones still standing when the door opens.

q: My 13-year-old has been asked to play up an age group. Good idea or too much?
a: It can be the making of a player or a slow leak in their confidence, and the difference is almost never the kid's talent — it's the role. So ask the coach the questions that matter: will he get real minutes, and what's his job in the team? Battling bigger bodies teaches heaps if he's on the floor; watching from the bench in an older group teaches almost nothing at thirteen. Then read your son honestly — excited-nervous is a green light, quiet dread is information. Ask whether a mix is possible, because plenty of associations allow it: play up for the stretch, stay in his own age group for the confidence reps and the mates. Agree on a trial window — four weeks, then you, he and the coach review it together — so nobody's locked into a decision made in week one. Most important bit: give him a real say. His buy-in is what decides whether playing up becomes growth or a grind.

q: I'm 24 and only started playing two years ago. Is proper competition out of reach?
a: Out of reach of the pros? Real talk, almost certainly — I won't sell you a fairytale. Out of reach of genuinely good, competitive basketball? Not even close, and this is the part people get wrong. Australia is stacked with graded social and domestic comps where the top divisions are seriously strong, and the pathway is simple: enter at your level, dominate it, move up a grade, repeat. Your advantage over every teenager in the gym is adult discipline — three structured sessions a week with tracked numbers will out-build talent that doesn't train, and you can hold that routine for years. Find runs where the players are better than you and be the guy who defends, passes and never complains; that guy gets invited back everywhere, and playing above your level is the fastest teacher there is. The honest answer is your ceiling is unknown, and unknown is the fun part. The game doesn't care when you arrived — only how you show up.

q: I play school ball and club ball and I'm cooked. Do I have to choose?
a: Maybe not choose, but definitely prioritise, because trying to run two programs at a hundred percent usually ends with flat performances in both. Map your week honestly on paper: games, trainings, schoolwork, sleep — and if sleep is the thing shrinking, that's your alarm bell, not a badge of honour. Then talk to both coaches, straight up. Good coaches would much rather manage your load than lose you mid-season, and most will coordinate once they know — a lighter Tuesday here, a rested game there. Pick one program as your priority for this season based on development, not loyalty: better coaching, harder competition, more real minutes — and protect that one when the calendar collides. Learn the difference between busy and better, because more games isn't more development if you're too cooked to sprint in any of them. A tired body playing everything beats nobody; a fresh body playing the right things beats plenty.

q: Tournament day — three games back-to-back. What do I actually eat between games?
a: Real talk: tournament days are won by the kid who fuels between games, not the kid who smashes one big feed at lunch and falls asleep in game three. The trick is small and often. Pack a bag the night before: things that are easy on the stomach and quick to digest — a banana, a sandwich cut in halves, crackers, a muesli bar, some fruit. Straight after each game, get a little something in and keep sipping water, don't wait until you feel hungry, because by then you're already behind. Save anything heavy or greasy for after the last buzzer — a big hot meal an hour before tip-off will sit in your guts like a brick. And here's the pattern I've seen over a lot of local basketball: the teams that look fresh in the last game of the day are almost always the ones with the organised food bag, not the ones raiding the canteen between rounds.

q: What should I eat at halftime? Some of my teammates eat lollies.
a: Halftime is short, so keep it simple: water first, then something small only if you actually need it. If you fuelled properly before the game, most players don't need to eat at all at halftime — a few good sips of water and you're right. If it's been a long day or you're feeling flat, a few orange slices, half a banana, or a couple of bites of a muesli bar can top you up without sitting heavy. The lolly thing? A small handful won't ruin anyone, but a big sugar hit can spike you up and drop you flat midway through the third — I've watched that movie plenty of times. Whatever you choose, test it at training first, never in a game that matters. The golden rule of game food: nothing new on game day.

q: My games finish at 9:30 at night. Is it bad to eat that late?
a: Here's the truth: your body doesn't check the clock before it decides whether it needs fuel. You just played a game — you need to eat, full stop, even if it's late. Skipping food after a night game because "eating late is bad" just means you wake up flat, cranky and running on empty at school the next day. Keep it sensible rather than skipping it: something with some carbs and protein in it — leftovers warmed up, a chicken wrap, eggs on toast, a big bowl of cereal with milk if that's all the energy you've got left to make. Have it soon after you get home, then wind down and get to bed, because sleep is the other half of recovery. Late food beats no food every single time for a player.

q: I get so nervous before games I can't eat anything. What do I do?
a: Youngblood, this is more common than you'd think — nerves shut the appetite down, it's just your body getting ready to compete. Don't force a big plate down, and don't play on empty either; the middle path is small, easy, familiar. Go for foods that slide down without a fight: a smoothie, a banana, yoghurt, a piece of toast with honey, and eat them a bit earlier than usual so there's less pressure closer to tip-off. Liquids are your mate here — if chewing feels impossible, drink your fuel. Then make it a routine: same simple pre-game snack every week, so your body learns "oh, this again, we know this" and the nerves have less to grab onto. If eating before games never gets easier or you're feeling sick with nerves all the time, loop in your GP — but for most players, small, familiar and early sorts it out.

q: My games are 8am Saturdays and I can't stomach food that early. Help?
a: Early games catch everyone out — nobody's stomach wants a feed at 6:45 in the morning. The fix starts the night before: a proper dinner Friday night does a lot of the heavy lifting, so you're not relying on breakfast to carry you. Morning of, don't aim for a big breakfast, aim for something — small and easy wins here. A banana, a slice of toast, a small bowl of cereal, a yoghurt, or a smoothie you can sip in the car on the way to the stadium all count. Sip water from the moment you wake up too, because you've been dry all night. Do the same routine every Saturday and I promise your body adjusts — the first few weeks feel rough, then one day eating at 7am is just what you do. Habits over highlights, even at breakfast.

q: I'm a mum of two junior players — what should I actually pack in the esky?
a: Love this question, because the esky is honestly one of the most underrated pieces of basketball equipment in the country. Think three jobs: water, between-game fuel, and after-game recovery. Water bottles for everyone, more than you think you need. For between games: fruit that travels well, sandwiches or wraps made that morning, crackers, muesli bars, yoghurt pouches if you've got ice bricks in there. For after the last game: something a bit more solid, like a chicken and salad roll or leftovers in a container, so the drive home doesn't turn into a starving-kids negotiation at the drive-through. Keep it stuff your kids already like and already eat — game day is not the day to introduce quinoa. The parents who pack the esky well save money at the canteen and hand their kids an edge in the afternoon games, simple as that.

q: My son only eats about five foods. How do I fuel him for basketball?
a: First up, no shame in this house — plenty of kids run on a short menu, and some kids' brains and bodies genuinely find new foods hard, I understand that better than most. Start by working with the five foods, not against them: if he eats pasta, toast, chicken nuggets, apples and milk, there's actually a workable base in there — carbs, protein, fruit, dairy. Serve the foods he trusts around training and games so he's fuelled, and keep new foods completely separate from basketball, zero pressure, just something new sitting on the table near something safe. Small exposures over months beat big battles over dinner every time — same as building any skill, it's reps, not force. Never turn food into a fight before a game; a fed kid on "beige food" outplays a stressed kid on nothing. And if the list is very short, he's dropping foods, or you're worried about how he's growing, that's the moment for your GP or an Accredited Sports Dietitian — they deal with fussy eating all the time and they won't judge either of you.

q: I'm vegetarian — can I still fuel properly for basketball?
a: Absolutely you can — there are strong vegetarian athletes at every level of this game, so let's kill that doubt straight away. The main job is making sure protein and iron don't quietly go missing when the meat leaves the plate. Get familiar with the vegetarian workhorses: eggs, dairy, beans, lentils, chickpeas, tofu, nuts, and get some of them into most meals rather than just eating the family dinner minus the meat. That last bit is the classic trap — pasta with no mince, stir-fry with no chicken, and suddenly you're training hard on half the fuel. Iron matters extra for busy young athletes, especially girls, so it's worth one proper conversation with your GP or an Accredited Sports Dietitian to check you're set up right — one visit, and you've got a plan for years. After that it's just habits: same as your jump shot, build the plate right often enough and it becomes automatic.

q: My parents work late on my training nights. What can I actually cook myself?
a: Respect for even asking, because feeding yourself properly is a genuine life skill and most adults I worked with over the years never mastered it. Start with a small rotation you can't mess up: eggs any way you like them on toast, pasta with a jar of sauce and a tin of tuna stirred through, a stir-fry with frozen veg and whatever protein is in the fridge, wraps with chicken and salad, or upgraded two-minute noodles with an egg cracked in and frozen peas thrown at it. Five go-to meals is all you need — that's your starting lineup, and you can add fancy stuff later. Ask whoever does the shopping to keep your ingredients stocked, and cook a bit extra when you can so tomorrow's dinner is already sitting in the fridge. Real talk: a teenager who can feed themselves after training will out-recover the kid waiting hungry on the couch for someone to get home. Reps in the kitchen count too.

q: I keep forgetting to drink water at school, then training feels terrible. Any tricks?
a: Here's the pattern: players think hydration is a training-time job, but if you rock up to a 4pm session dry from a whole school day, no water bottle on the bench is saving you — you're playing catch-up all night. So make it a habit problem, not a willpower problem. Carry a bottle you actually like using, keep it on your desk where you can see it, and anchor drinking to things that already happen: every time you change classes, sip; recess and lunch, proper drink; bell rings, sip. That's it — you're not counting anything, you're just attaching water to your existing routine, same way we attach habits to triggers in training. Easy self-check: if you're barely going to the toilet all day or it's dark when you do, you're running dry. Fix the school-day habit and watch how different that first ten minutes of training feels.

q: The whole team gets maccas after every game. Do I have to say no?
a: Here's the truth: I'm never going to tell you to skip the team feed, because sitting around with your teammates laughing about the game is part of why we play. Community over clout, and honestly, over perfect eating too. One post-game maccas run in a week where you're training well and eating decent food at home is not the thing holding your game back — don't let anyone shame you over it. Where it goes sideways is when the exception becomes the routine: fast food after every game, every training, every weekend, and suddenly it's most of your fuel. So go, order a normal feed instead of the biggest thing on the menu, grab water or a drink you'd actually be fine with, and enjoy your mates. Balance means the food fits around your goals most of the time — not that you sit in the car alone while the boys eat inside.

q: Sports drinks or water — when does each one actually make sense?
a: Straight answer: water covers you for almost everything a junior or social baller does. Normal training session, one game on the weekend — water before, during and after is all the hydration you need, and it's free. Sports drinks earn their spot in a narrower window: long, hot, sweaty days where you're playing multiple games or training for hours and sweating buckets — that's when the extra carbs and salts they carry actually do the job they were designed for. Sipping them on the couch, at school, or through a regular one-hour session is just sugar you didn't need, dressed up in sports marketing. I've watched a lot of local basketball, and the bottle on the bench matters way less than whether you drank anything at all that day. So: water as your default, sports drink as a tool for the big hot tournament days — not a personality.

q: I keep cramping up in the last quarter. What's going on?
a: Cramps are your body waving a flag, and the honest answer is nobody can tell you from a distance exactly which flag it is. The common culprits are simple: not enough water through the day, playing big minutes in the heat, going hard on an empty tank, or your body just working beyond what it's currently conditioned for. So check the basics first — are you drinking through the school day and not just at the game, did you eat properly beforehand, are you warming up right, and are you suddenly playing way more minutes than usual? Often tightening up those habits sorts it. But here's the rail I won't move on: if you're cramping regularly, it's one-sided, it's painful beyond the moment, or the basics don't fix it, get it looked at by your GP — and an Accredited Sports Dietitian can check the fuel side properly. Cramps are information. Don't just stretch them out and ignore the message.

q: Night game tonight, training tomorrow morning. How do I recover in time?
a: Back-to-backs are where recovery habits actually get tested — anyone can recover with a free day, but this is the real exam. The window straight after the game matters most: eat something with carbs and protein soon after the final buzzer, even if it's late and even if it's simple — a wrap, leftovers, cereal and milk, whatever's realistic at that hour. Keep drinking water through the evening too, because you'll be tempted to just crash. Then protect your sleep like it's your starting spot: shower, food, screens down, bed — the scrolling can wait, your body's doing its repair work overnight and it needs the hours. In the morning, get some breakfast in before the session even if it's small, and expect to feel a bit rusty in the warm-up; that's normal, work through it honestly. Slow the mind, fuel the body, and tomorrow-you will thank tonight-you.

q: I'm always flat and tired at training lately, even when I sleep okay. Why?
a: When a player goes flat for a week, I look at habits; when a player stays flat for weeks, I stop guessing and send them to a professional — and that's my honest answer for you too. Run the pattern check first: are you actually eating enough for how much you're training, especially breakfast and lunch on school days? Are you drinking water through the day? Has your load jumped — new team, extra sessions, exams stacked on top? Growing teenagers doing sport burn serious fuel, and "always tired" is often just "always under-fuelled" wearing a disguise. But constant fatigue can also be things I'm not qualified to see — low iron is a classic in young athletes — so if this has been hanging around for a few weeks, tell your parents and get to your GP, and an Accredited Sports Dietitian can look at the fuel side. Pushing through week after week isn't tough, it's just training badly with extra steps. Get it checked.

q: After a bad loss I don't feel like eating dinner. Is that a problem?
a: I get it — a rough loss can kill your appetite stone dead, and food feels like the last thing that matters. But here's the truth: your body doesn't know you lost. It just knows it played a full game and it needs fuel to repair, same as after a win. Skipping dinner doesn't punish the loss, it just punishes tomorrow's version of you — flatter at school, flatter at the next session, slower to bounce back. So separate the two things: feel whatever you feel about the game, that's allowed, but feed the athlete anyway, even if it's something small and easy. A loss is information for your next session, not a reason to run yourself down — process over outcome applies at the dinner table too. One more thing, and I mean this seriously: if skipping meals after bad games is becoming a pattern, or food is starting to feel tied up with punishment and performance, talk to your parents and your GP about it. That's a knot worth untangling early, with proper help.

q: Money's tight at home. How do I eat well for basketball on a small budget?
a: First, respect to your family — and hear this clearly: good fuel is not about expensive food, no matter what social media tells you. Some of the best athlete food in the supermarket is the cheapest stuff there: eggs, oats, rice, pasta, tinned tuna, frozen vegetables, bananas, milk, bread, lentils and beans. A big pot of pasta with mince and frozen veg, fried rice with egg, or tuna and rice bowls will fuel training as well as anything from a fancy meal service. Skip the "athlete" branded stuff entirely — protein bars, sports drinks and powders are where budgets go to die, and water plus real food beats them anyway. Cook big and stretch it: one large cook-up becomes dinner tonight and tomorrow's post-training meal. Tap water, home brand everything, whatever fruit and veg is on special that week — that's not settling, that's smart. I've watched plenty of great players come out of households doing it tough; the fuel was simple, it was just there consistently. Consistency is the whole game.

q: How do I meal prep for a heavy training week without it taking over my life?
a: Keep it boring and it'll actually last — that's the secret nobody selling containers wants to tell you. You don't need seven colour-coded lunches; you need to remove decisions from your busiest days. Pick one cooking window, usually Sunday, and do three things: cook a big batch of a base like rice or pasta, cook one protein in bulk like a tray of chicken or a pot of mince, and make sure there's easy veg around, frozen absolutely counts. Now every training night is assembly, not cooking — base plus protein plus veg, five minutes, done. Add grab-and-go snacks to your bag the night before so post-school hunger doesn't ambush you into the canteen. Think of it like film study for your week: a bit of prep up front so game time runs smooth. Start with prepping just your training days, not the whole week — a small system you actually repeat beats a perfect one you quit by Wednesday.

q: Are frozen and canned veggies worse for my kids than fresh ones?
a: Real talk: no, and this myth costs families money every single week. Frozen vegetables are usually snap-frozen right after picking, so they hold their goodness extremely well — often better than "fresh" veg that's spent a week travelling and another week in your crisper drawer going soft. Canned is solid too; just give things like beans and corn a quick rinse if you want less salt. For a sporting family, frozen and canned are honestly a cheat code: cheaper, no waste because nothing rots in the fridge, and always there at 8:30pm when training ran late and everyone's starving. The vegetables your kids actually eat beat the perfect vegetables that die in the fridge, every time. So buy fresh when it's in season and on special, and let the freezer and pantry carry the rest of the week without an ounce of guilt. Feeding young athletes is about showing up consistently, not showing off.

q: I blow all my pocket money at the stadium canteen every weekend. Is that bad?
a: The canteen trap is real, my guy — hot chips smell like victory and they've got you rocking up hungry with money in your pocket. Let's be clear first: canteen food isn't evil, and a bag of chips at the stadium sometimes is just part of Saturday basketball in this country. The problem is when the canteen becomes your whole game-day fuel plan — greasy, heavy food between games sits in your stomach, costs a fortune, and by game three you're broke and flat. So flip the setup: eat before you leave home, pack your own between-game food and a full water bottle, and now the canteen becomes a treat you choose instead of a trap you fall into because you're starving. Buy the chips after your last game if you want them — they taste better as a reward anyway. You'll play better and your pocket money might actually survive the weekend. That's a double win.

q: Do I need protein powder after training, or is normal food enough?
a: Here's the truth, and it's cheaper than what the supplement shop will tell you: for a young player, real food does the job. Protein powder isn't magic — it's just protein in a tub, and you can get the same thing from milk, eggs, yoghurt, chicken, tuna, beans, cheese on toast. The industry is brilliant at making teenagers feel like they're missing a secret; you're not. Where shakes genuinely help adults is convenience, not power — and even then, food first is the principle. For you, the better post-training move is simply having real food ready to go, because the kid who eats a proper meal after every session beats the kid with the fancy shaker and empty fridge. And because you're still growing, this is a hard rule from me: before you spend a cent on any powder, run it past your GP or an Accredited Sports Dietitian — they'll tell you straight whether you need it, and nine times out of ten they'll point you back at the fridge.

q: My gym mates say creatine is totally safe and I should start. Should I?
a: I'm going to give you the straight answer your mates can't: this is not a decision for the group chat. Creatine is one of the most researched supplements around — in adults. For teenagers who are still growing, the honest position is that this belongs with a professional, not with whichever mate read the most Reddit threads. There's also a real-world problem nobody at the gym mentions: supplements aren't all made equal, and some products contain things that aren't on the label — that's a genuine risk when you're young and buying whatever's cheapest online. Here's what I know from thirty years around the game: no supplement has ever turned an average trainer into a player, but consistent food, sleep and reps have done it thousands of times. Get those three dialled first, because they're the actual foundation. Then, if you're still curious, take the question to your GP or an Accredited Sports Dietitian and let someone qualified look at you specifically. That's not the boring answer — that's the strong answer.

q: Can I have an energy drink before games? Heaps of guys at my comp do.
a: Youngblood, I'm going to be straight with you: energy drinks and growing bodies are a bad mix, and "heaps of guys do it" has never once made something a good idea. Those cans carry serious caffeine loads built for adults, and in teenagers that can mean a racing heart, jitters, rubbish sleep that night, and a nasty crash — sometimes right in the middle of your game. Here's the thing the can won't tell you: real energy doesn't come from a drink, it comes from sleeping properly, eating before you play, and drinking water through the day. The buzz you feel isn't extra energy, it's borrowed energy with interest. Caffeine for teens is genuinely a talk-to-your-GP topic, so if you're leaning on these drinks to get through games or school, that's the conversation to have — especially if you've noticed your sleep falling apart. Fix the fuel and the sleep, and I promise you won't miss the can. Slow the mind, speed the body — a heart rattling from caffeine does the exact opposite.

q: Should I take pre-workout before training? The gym guys swear by it.
a: Real talk: pre-workout is mostly caffeine wearing a costume, and for a teenager that's a no from me until a professional says otherwise. Those tubs are dosed for grown adults, the tingly feeling isn't power, and some of the cheaper ones contain ingredients that wouldn't pass a sniff test — that's not a gamble worth taking with a growing body. But let's talk about what you're actually chasing, because that part is legit: you want to walk into training with energy and intent. You can build that without a scoop of anything. Eat something real an hour or two before, sip water through the day, get your sleep right, and build a switch-on routine — same warm-up, same first drills, maybe some music on the way in. That routine becomes your pre-workout, and it's free and it travels everywhere with you. If you still feel like you need something extra just to train, that's worth a chat with your GP or an Accredited Sports Dietitian — needing a stimulant to move is a flag, not a flex.

q: Should my 14-year-old be taking a multivitamin for basketball?
a: Good on you for asking before buying, because the supplement aisle is built to make sporting parents feel like they're one purchase short. Here's the honest position: for most kids eating a reasonable spread of food, a multivitamin is expensive insurance for a problem they don't have — the body takes what it needs from food and the rest, to put it politely, goes down the toilet. Vitamins work best arriving the way nature packages them: in meals, spread across the day. Where it changes is if there's a genuine gap — a very restricted eater, a vegetarian or vegan diet, certain health conditions, or a GP finds something like low iron in a blood test. But that's exactly the point: a real gap should be found and filled by your GP or an Accredited Sports Dietitian, not guessed at in aisle five. If you're unsure, book the appointment instead of buying the bottle — it's cheaper in the long run and you'll actually know. Then spend the savings on decent groceries and a good water bottle. That's the real supplement stack for a 14-year-old.

q: I'm 15 and skinny. How do I bulk up for basketball without supplements?
a: First, breathe — at 15 your body is still writing its own story, and I've watched plenty of skinny teenagers turn into strong twenty-year-olds without a single scoop of anything. The food-first truth is that getting stronger while growing mostly comes down to eating enough, consistently: three proper meals, snacks between them, and never training on empty or skipping the meal after. Most "hardgainers" I've seen weren't cursed, they were just accidentally under-eating for how much sport and growing they were doing at the same time. So build the habits: breakfast every day non-negotiable, food in your bag for after school, a real dinner, milk instead of nothing. Pair it with your strength work and give it months, not weeks — patience is a skill, same as your handle. And because you're growing, do this properly: a chat with your GP or an Accredited Sports Dietitian gets you a plan built for your body instead of a random one off YouTube. Strong is built slowly, mate. The players who rush it with shortcuts usually end up back at the start.

q: Ramadan is coming and I've got games and training. How do I manage fasting and basketball?
a: Respect first — plenty of ballers fast and play every year, and it can absolutely be done with some planning and some honesty about your limits. The two meals become everything: don't sleep through suhoor, make it count with slow-burning food that'll carry you, and at iftar break the fast gently, rehydrate properly through the evening, and get a solid meal in rather than just sweets and a scramble to bed. Where you can, shift your harder sessions towards the evening near iftar so the fuel and water aren't a full day away, and be upfront with your coach about what's on — any decent coach will work with you, and it's a chance for your teammates to understand something about you too. Listen hard to your body on court: dizzy, faint or unwell is your signal to stop, not push through, no game is worth that. And do have a chat with your GP before the month, especially if you're young, still growing, or carrying a big training load — they can help you set it up safely for your situation, alongside the guidance of your family and community. Fasting builds discipline, and discipline is the backbone of every good player I've ever seen.

q: My 13-year-old is suddenly eating everything in the house. Is this normal for a young athlete?
a: Ha — welcome to the growth spurt plus basketball combo, the most expensive phase of parenting a young athlete. Yes, this is normal, and honestly it's a good sign: a growing body doing regular sport is running two energy bills at once, and the hunger is just the invoice. The worst thing you can do is make a kid feel greedy or wrong for it — fuel, don't restrict, is the rule for growing bodies, full stop. Your job isn't to slow the eating down, it's to point it at decent food: keep easy real food where the hunger strikes — fruit on the bench, yoghurt and cheese in the fridge, bread and eggs always stocked, big dinners with seconds available. If the pantry only offers packets, packets are what a starving teenager will eat, so stock the good stuff at ambush height. Buy in bulk, cook in bulk, and know this phase passes. And if anything ever seems off — eating heaps but always exhausted, or big weight changes that worry you — that's a GP conversation, just to be safe. Otherwise, keep the fridge full and enjoy the grocery bills, mate. It means the engine's working.

q: I feel bigger than the other girls on my team. Should I go on a diet?
a: Here's the truth, and I need you to actually hear it: no. You're growing, and growing bodies come in different shapes on different timelines — comparing yours to your teammates' is like comparing two plants in different seasons and deciding one of them is wrong. Dieting as a teenager doesn't build athletes; it drains them — the energy, the focus, the bounce in your legs all run on fuel, and restricting it is how good players go backwards. The rule in my book for every growing player is fuel, don't restrict: eat proper meals, eat around your training, and let your body do the building it's designed to do right now. Basketball has never had one body type anyway — the game needs strength, and strong comes in a lot of shapes. If worries about your body or food are taking up real space in your head, please don't carry that alone: talk to your parents and your GP, and an Accredited Sports Dietitian can show you how to fuel as an athlete without any of the diet rubbish. Your body is the equipment your game runs on. Feed it like you respect it, because I promise the players who do go furthest.

q: My 12-year-old wants to eat like the pros he watches. What actually matters at his age?
a: I love the enthusiasm, and here's the good news: what matters at 12 is beautifully boring. Pro athletes have chefs, dietitians and recovery staff; your son needs breakfast every day, real food in his lunchbox, water instead of soft drink most of the time, a decent dinner, and enough sleep — that IS eating like a pro at his age, because the pros are just doing the fundamentals with a bigger budget. Skip anything that comes in a tub or promises performance; at 12 that stuff ranges from pointless to genuinely not appropriate, and any supplement question for a kid belongs with your GP, not a shop assistant. Use his motivation where it counts: let him help cook, let him pack his own game-day bag, teach him that showing up fuelled is part of being serious. That's pattern-building he'll carry for life — habits over highlights. And gently keep food fun, not a performance project; a 12-year-old who enjoys eating with his family is set up better than one already stressing over every plate. The fundamentals win. They always do.

q: I play scared of stuffing up, so I hide on court and barely touch the ball.
a: Real talk: coaches bench hesitation way more often than they bench mistakes. When you hide, you're making a mistake every possession — it's just an invisible one. So give yourself a job that has nothing to do with scoring: in your first five minutes, get one deflection, one hard cut, and make one loud call. None of those can be 'stuffed up', and all of them drag you into the game. Then adopt my rule: aggressive mistakes are free this month. Turn it over driving hard? Fine. Get beat playing up on your man? Fine. Your brain learns pretty quick that the ball doesn't explode when you make a play, and that's when the real player comes out of hiding.

q: I dropped a heap of points on the weekend and now I feel untouchable. Is that bad?
a: Enjoy it — you earned the night. Then here's the truth: you get 24 hours, and after that the big game becomes homework. Watch the footage back and find three plays you got away with — a lazy closeout, a pass that should've been picked, a shot that was luckier than it looked. They're always there. Because here's what changed on the weekend: teams scout now. The next opponent is planning for you, and 'untouchable' is exactly the mindset they want you carrying in. In chess, winning one game doesn't make you a grandmaster — it makes you someone worth studying. Habits over highlights, mate. The players who last treat their best game as the new floor to work from, not a throne to sit on.

q: I'm the quiet one on my team and I can't bring myself to talk on court.
a: Good news, youngblood: talking on court is a skill, not a personality type. Nobody's asking you to become the loud kid — they're asking you to pass information, and quiet players are often the best at it because they're actually watching. Start with three scripted calls that mean something: 'shot', 'help left', 'screen coming'. You're not making conversation, you're reading out what you see — no cleverness required. Set yourself a target of one call per defensive possession and count them like you'd count rebounds. The first few feel weird coming out of your mouth; by week three they're automatic, and your teammates start trusting the quiet kid's voice more than the loud one's, because yours only speaks when it's true.

q: I've been made captain but I'm not loud. How am I supposed to lead?
a: Here's the truth about leadership that took me years of ball to learn: teams follow standards, not volume. The loudest player is rarely the leader — he's just the loudest player. You lead by being first to every drill, sprinting back on defence when you're gassed, and telling a teammate 'great pass' when everyone else only noticed the finish. Then use your actual superpower: quiet one-on-one words. 'You right, mate? Next play' said privately to a struggling teammate is worth ten huddle speeches. Think chess — the queen doesn't shout, she just shows up everywhere it matters. Set the standard with your body, protect teammates with your words, and let the scoreboard do the yelling.

q: I'm one of the best in my comp and now every team doubles and targets me.
a: First, understand what's happening: being targeted is a compliment written in defensive schemes. They're spending two players on you, which means — do the maths — somebody on your team is standing free every single possession. So change what a good game means. Some nights your best stat line is eight assists and a tired defender chasing you round screens, because the double is a chess move and the correct answer is the pass, not the hero dribble through three blokes. Study the pattern: where does the second defender come from, and when? That's information you can use by half-time. And keep your face boring — targets who get frustrated get targeted harder. Stay calm, keep passing, and make them pay for the compliment until they stop paying it.

q: I played great all season and then froze in the grand final. What happened to me?
a: Nothing broke, mate — your brain just decided that game was 'bigger', so it stopped running your process and started watching the outcome like a nervous spectator. That's what choking actually is, and it's happened to players at every level you can name. The fix is making finals feel like rounds. Same warm-up, same music, same first-five-minutes job — a rebound, a stop, a hard cut — so your body gets told 'this is just basketball' before your head can argue. Then shrink the game: never play the grand final, only play the next possession, forty times in a row. And between now and the next big one, rehearse pressure at training — free throws where a miss costs you sprints, scrimmages with a countdown clock and a scenario. Pressure is a skill you can rep like anything else. One frozen final is a lesson, not a diagnosis.

q: I'm scared of the last shot — I always pass it off even when I'm open.
a: Real talk: you're not scared of the shot, you're scared of the story after the miss. So let's fix the story first — every great shooter in history has missed a pile of game-winners, and their careers survived. Now train the moment so it stops being special: end every session with ten 'game-winners', legs tired, counting down out loud from five, moving to your spot off a catch. You're teaching your body this is just another rep. Then make the decision before the game, not during it: 'if I'm open in my spot with the game on the line, it's going up.' Deciding early means the moment can't ask you the question. One more thing — passing to a wide-open teammate is the right play and always will be. Passing because your stomach flipped is the tell. Learn to know which one you just did.

q: I keep losing my temper mid-game — snapping at refs and my own teammates.
a: Anger on court means you care, but let's be honest about the price: techs, benched minutes, teammates who stop looking for you. Start with the refs — they're humans doing their best in a hard job, and in thirty years of ball I've never once seen arguing change a call. Not once. So build a physical reset that beats the flash of heat: walk to the free-throw line, hands on your shorts, one slow breath out, then say your word — mine's 'next'. That's five seconds, and it works because it gives your body a job before your mouth finds one. Then channel it: anger is fuel, and defence is the legal place to burn it — chase the loose ball, take the charge, make your man feel it within the rules. And if you notice the fuse is short everywhere lately, not just on court, that's worth an honest chat with someone you trust — a parent, a coach, someone solid. Temper is a pattern, and patterns can be trained.

q: I'm fine shooting in an empty gym but a big crowd throws me right off.
a: Crowds are weather, mate — you can't control them, so you learn to play in the rain. First, narrow the world: rim, ball, your man. The crowd lives outside those three things, and your eyes decide what gets in. Second, understand crowd physics: they react to the last thing that happened, but you live in the next thing — by the time they're roaring about your miss, you should already be back on defence where the noise can't follow.
