Third, train for it: shoot free throws with music blasting and your mates chirping rubbish at you, so a noisy gym isn't a new experience on game night. And get physical early — a rebound, a screen, a bump in the first two minutes tells your nervous system it's just basketball. The empty-gym player is still in there; you're just teaching him to perform with witnesses.

q: Opponents trash talk me all game and it gets right inside my head.
a: Here's what trash talk actually is: a scouting report on your temper. They do it because somewhere, sometime, it worked on you — and word travels. The best answer ever invented is silence plus scoreboard, so build a routine for the moment it lands: small smile, walk away, call the next play like they never spoke. Do not return fire — the second you chirp back you're playing their game on their board, and in chess you never let the opponent pick the opening. What kills a trash talker isn't a comeback, it's irrelevance: bloke's been yapping for three quarters and you haven't looked at him once. Now, one serious line: if it crosses from banter into racist or genuinely personal abuse, that's not trash talk anymore — tell your coach and the ref straight away, because handling that is an adult's job, not yours.

q: I barely get minutes and spend most games cheering from the bench. How do I stay ready?
a: First, respect where you are: every rotation player you've ever admired did bench time, and the ones who made it treated that seat like a classroom, not a waiting room. So scout from it — watch the player you'd sub in for, learn his matchup, notice what the defence gives up, so when your name gets called you arrive with answers. Stay physically ready too: stand at every timeout, stay warm, be first off the bench celebrating — coaches absolutely count energy as a stat, I promise you. Then here's the move that changes careers: when you do get your three minutes, do the unglamorous things violently well — defend, sprint, screen, talk. Coaches extend minutes for players they can trust at random, and trust is built in exactly those cameos. The dark work always gets found. Always.

q: I catch myself training for clips for my page instead of actually getting better.
a: Respect for catching it, because most don't — the camera changes what you practise, and the algorithm loves a crossover way more than the game does. Here's the truth: the internet rewards highlights, but games are won by the boring stuff nobody films — footwork, left hand, closeouts, the four hundredth catch-and-shoot. So make a rule with yourself: the first fifty minutes of every session are unfilmed, and only the last ten can go on the phone. Judge your week by reps done, not likes gained — write the numbers down where you can see them. And if you want to really flip it, post the boring stuff sometimes: the missed reps, the conditioning, the 6am gym. That's the content the players you respect actually respect. Habits over highlights — it's not just a saying, it's the whole game.

q: I stay up late gaming and I'm absolutely cooked at morning trainings.
a: I'm not going to tell you to bin the console — that lecture never works and you'd stop reading. But here's what nobody tells you: sleep is where training actually becomes improvement, so a late night doesn't just make you tired, it partly wastes yesterday's session. Run an experiment on yourself for two weeks, proper pattern recognition: write down what time you switched off and rate the next morning's training out of ten. The pattern will slap you in the face, and it'll be your data, not my nagging. Then set a kick-out time — controller down at a set hour, and put the phone across the room so the scroll can't ambush you in bed. Game hard, sleep hard, train hard. The order matters.

q: In the off-season nobody's checking on me and my training just falls apart.
a: That's because you're relying on discipline as a feeling, and feelings sleep in. The players who train year-round have a system doing the heavy lifting instead. Shrink the plan until it's almost embarrassing — three sessions a week, written on paper, stuck where you see it every morning — because a small plan you actually do beats the massive one you abandon by week two. Then borrow accountability: tell a mate the plan, or better, train with someone, because it's easy to ghost a court but hard to ghost a person standing on it. Track your streak somewhere visible and adopt the golden rule: never miss twice. Missing one session is life; missing two in a row is a new habit forming, and it's forming against you. Off-seasons are where next season's rotation quietly gets decided.

q: A couple of teammates whinge and sulk all game and it's dragging the whole team down.
a: Energy is contagious in both directions, mate — that's just how teams work — so the first job is making sure you're not catching it. Decide you're the counter-signal: loud on effort plays, first to pick a bloke up off the floor, next-play voice after mistakes. Then recruit, because one positive player is an exception but three is a culture: get a teammate or two to deliberately match your energy and you outnumber the mood without a single lecture. If one of the whingers matters to you, have the quiet word one-on-one, never in front of the group — 'we're better when you're up, we need you' lands, while public callouts just create a new sulk. And if it's genuinely poisoning the team, that's a respectful conversation for your captain and coach to own, not something to carry alone. Protect your own game first; you can't pour from an empty tank.

q: Coach dropped me from the starting five and I'm gutted. What now?
a: Feel it tonight — being gutted means you care, and I'd be worried if you weren't. But tomorrow you go to work, and step one is a respectful question, not a protest: 'Coach, what do you need to see from me to earn the spot back?' Then — and this is where most players fail — you do that thing, not the thing you'd rather do. Here's what thirty years of ball taught me about this exact moment: coaches watch how you respond to being dropped far more closely than they watched the form dip that caused it. So for the next fortnight, be undeniable: first to every drill, loudest on the bench, defence like your spot depends on it, because it does. And remember starting is a role, not an identity — plenty of players finish games instead of starting them and matter more for it. Sulking has never won a spot back in the history of the sport. Work has, thousands of times.

q: The physio cleared me after months out injured, but my head's still not right on court.
a: First things first: the body call belongs to your physio and GP, full stop — if they've cleared you, that box is ticked, and if anything hurts you go straight back to them. What you're describing is the part nobody warns you about: the head heals slower than the body. That hesitation isn't weakness, it's your brain being an overprotective parent, and you retrain it with evidence, not pep talks. So feed it proof: controlled reps of the exact movement you're scared of, contact drills built up gradually, then short minutes with one simple job — defend and run the floor — before you ask yourself to be the old you. Confidence comes back on reps, not on the calendar, so stop checking the date and start counting the evidence. And if the fear is still running your game months down the track, a session with a psychologist who works with athletes is a strength move — pros do it all the time, and so should we.

q: I'm fifteen and I sometimes cry after losses. Is that weak?
a: Real talk: no. Crying after a loss means you invested everything and it didn't pay out — that's the receipt for caring, not a weakness. Grown professionals cry in sheds after grand finals every single season, in footy and basketball both, and nobody sound calls them soft. So don't fight the feeling; give it a structure instead. Let it out on the night — fully, no shame — and then set a debrief window: next day, three questions on paper. What did I do well? What actually cost us? What am I training on Monday because of it? That turns the hurt into fuel instead of letting it just sit there as hurt. And one honest line from your UNC: if the sadness hangs around for weeks after a game, that's bigger than basketball, and it deserves a conversation with someone you trust — a parent, a school counsellor, someone solid.

q: Basketball used to be my whole life, but lately I feel nothing when I play.
a: First, nothing is wrong with you. Love for the game breathes — it swells and it fades — and usually when it goes quiet it's not dead, it's buried under something: pressure, expectation, too many structured sessions, the game turning into a job. So dig it out. Take one session a week and strip every ounce of performance from it: pickup with mates, music on, silly shots, absolutely no coach's voice in your head. You're trying to find the driveway feeling — the reason nine-year-old you begged to stay out past dark. Funny thing I've seen over and over: the love usually walks back in the moment performance leaves the room. Give it a few weeks of playing for nothing before you make any big calls. And if the flatness sits over everything — school, mates, home, not just ball — for weeks on end, that's not a basketball problem, and it's worth telling someone you trust.

q: I've been seriously thinking about quitting basketball and I feel lost about it.
a: Heavy one, and I'm glad you brought it here instead of sitting on it alone. First truth: quitting a sport is allowed. People step away and come back stronger, and people step away and find something else that lights them up — neither one makes you a failure, and your worth was never tied to a jumper. But make the call from clarity, not exhaustion: ask yourself whether it's actually the game you want to leave, or the stuff wrapped around it — a coach, the pressure, the schedule, being flogged tired. Those are very different problems with very different fixes, and plenty of players who 'hated basketball' really just hated their situation. Either way, don't carry this solo — talk it through with a parent or an adult you trust before you decide anything. And if the lost feeling is bigger than basketball — if it follows you everywhere — call Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800. It's free, it's 24/7 for anyone under 25, and talking to them is a strong move, not a weak one.

q: My older brother is better at ball than me and everyone compares us. It stings.
a: Course it stings — sibling comparison is the hardest kind because you can't log off from it; it's at the dinner table. But let me reframe what you've actually got: a live-in training partner who's better than you, which is exactly what every developing player pays money and petrol to find. Use him. Ask him to hammer your weaknesses one-on-one, steal his habits, study what makes him effective — younger siblings who train against better competition their whole childhood have a long history of catching up and going past. Then fix your measuring stick: you versus him is a comparison you didn't choose, but you versus you-last-month is one you control completely, so track that instead. And tell him it stings sometimes — genuinely, brothers can handle that honesty, and he probably has no idea. The comparisons from other people fade in a few years. The training partner, you keep for life.

q: Exams are coming up and they clash with training. Which one do I skip?
a: Real talk, and you already know it: in a straight head-to-head, exams win, and any coach worth playing for will say the same thing before you finish the sentence. But handle it like a pro, not a ghost — tell your coach early and specifically: 'exam block these two weeks, back full tilt on this date.' Coaches forgive absence; they don't forgive vanishing. Then don't stop, downshift: twenty minutes of ball-handling or shooting as your study break, because movement genuinely freshens the head for the next study session — you're not stealing from study, you're topping it up. Timetable both, on paper, so neither one runs on guilt. Here's the bit nobody tells you: the discipline to shut the books and train, then shut the ball away and study, is the exact same muscle. Exam block is a rep for it.

q: Basketball is all I think about and my grades are sliding. Is that a problem?
a: I love the obsession, youngblood — you can't teach that, and I won't talk you out of it. But respect the maths: a tiny fraction of players earn a living from ball, and every single one of them still needed a working brain and a plan B, because careers end and life is long. School isn't the enemy of your hoop dream; it's the insurance policy protecting future-you. So cut a deal with yourself: schoolwork earns court time. Homework done, then the session — same day, every day, no exceptions. And here's the trick: you already have elite focus, you're just spending it all on one thing, so point that same obsessive energy at forty-five minutes of study and watch it wilt under the pressure. One more move: show your parents the plan before your grades force them to write one for you. Theirs will have a lot less basketball in it.

q: I play rep, school comp and social ball year-round and I've started dreading training.
a: Listen closely, because that dread is not weakness — it's a smoke alarm. Even the pros get an off-season, and you've built a schedule with no exhale in it: body and mind never get the rebuild window, and dread is what chronic no-rest feels like from the inside. So sit down with your parents and coaches and prune, respectfully but honestly: which team matters most for where you're heading, and which one can go? Fewer teams played hungry beats three teams played hollow, every time. Then book a genuine rest block — a couple of weeks a year where basketball is only something you watch — and write it in like it's training, because it is training; rest is where the gains land. If the exhaustion hangs around for weeks even after proper rest, get your GP to give you a once-over, just to rule things out. Protect the love, mate. It's the engine for everything else.

q: My mates are out every weekend while I'm training. Am I missing out on my twenties?
a: Honest answer from an old head: a bit, yes — and that's a real cost, so let's not pretend otherwise. But discipline doesn't have to mean isolation; that's a false choice that burns people out. Schedule your social life the way you schedule sessions: pick the nights that matter — the birthdays, the ones you'd genuinely regret missing — and be fully there, phone away, no guilt about the gym. Skip the filler nights that are just scrolling in a louder room. Then run the Monday test: how do you feel after a training weekend versus a big one out? Not what looks better on someone's story — how do you actually feel? Let that answer guide the ratio. And keep this close: the game itself is community — your teammates, the pickup regulars, the bloke you always match up on. Don't become the guy with a beautiful jump shot and nobody to text. Community over clout cuts both ways.

q: My coach yells constantly and it's really getting in my head. How do I cope?
a: First, a reframe that helps: some coaches only have one volume, and loud usually means invested — the players they've given up on are the ones they go quiet on. So learn to translate: inside every yell there's an instruction, and your job is to grab the instruction and let the volume fall on the floor. 'GET BACK ON DEFENCE' is just 'get back on defence' with the treble up. Practise hearing it that way and half the sting goes. If it's still living in your head, have a respectful conversation away from the court: 'Coach, I want your feedback — I just take it in better when it's direct rather than loud.' Most coaches genuinely respect a player mature enough to say that, and plenty have no idea how they're landing. One clear line though: loud coaching about basketball is one thing, but if it tips into personal put-downs or making you dread showing up, tell your parents — that conversation belongs to the adults.

q: My coach never gives me any feedback at all — good or bad. What do I do?
a: Here's a secret from my years training people for a living: silence is rarely disapproval — plenty of coaches only speak up when something's broken, so quiet can actually mean 'no problems here'. But you shouldn't have to guess, so go get your feedback instead of waiting for it. After training, one specific question: 'Coach, what's one thing I should work on for my role?' Specific is the key — 'how am I going?' invites a shrug, but 'one thing for my role' almost always gets a real answer, because you've made it easy. Then do the thing that separates you from everyone else who's ever asked: visibly work on it for a fortnight and report back. 'Been working on that closeout footwork you mentioned — what do you reckon?' You've just turned a silent coach into a coaching relationship, and he'll start volunteering feedback because he knows you use it. In the meantime, film your games and self-scout — the footage never goes quiet on you.

q: The car ride home after games is either dead silence or criticism from my dad.
a: This one's so common it should have its own name, so let me give you both sides straight. That silence is usually a parent who cares massively and has no idea what to say; the criticism is usually love wearing the wrong jacket — he thinks he's helping you improve. Knowing that doesn't make the car feel better, but it tells you this is fixable, because the problem is the timing and the script, not the love. So have the conversation — never in the car, never after a game, but on a calm night: 'Dad, I love that you come to every game. Straight after, my head's still in it and the criticism lands really hard. Can the car just be the car, and we talk basketball tomorrow if you've got thoughts?' Most parents have never once been told what actually helps, and most adjust more than you'd expect. Then give him a job, because he needs one: ask him to tell you the one play he enjoyed watching. That's it. You might just get your dad back on those drives.

q: I'm a mum of a thirteen-year-old baller — how do I support her without becoming the pushy sports parent?
a: The fact you're asking means you're already miles ahead of the parents who should be. Here's the gold standard, and it's six words: 'I love watching you play.' Before games, after games, after shockers — that's the whole speech, and kids can quote it back years later. Let her bring the basketball to you: if she wants to talk tactics in the kitchen, brilliant, go for it — but ask about her mates and the fun before you ever ask about the score. Leave technique to the coaches, one voice only, because a kid getting corrected from the sideline and the car and the coach ends up hearing nobody. Your jobs are the lifts, the food, the fees, and being exactly the same warm person after her worst game as her best — that consistency is the thing she'll actually remember at thirty. And keep one quiet check running: whose engine is this? If she's driving and you're supporting, perfect. The day you notice you're dragging her to sessions she'd rather skip, ease off and let her find the want again. It's her game, mum. You've got the best seat in the house.

q: I coach under-14s and one kid completely shuts down whenever I correct him.
a: Good on you for noticing, coach — plenty don't, and here's what my years in learning and development taught me about exactly this: some people receive correction as 'here's the fix' and others receive it as 'you're failing', and that second kid isn't soft, he's just wired to read feedback as a verdict on him. Usually he's the one who cares the most. So change the delivery, not the standard. Correct him privately, never in front of the group — walk past in a drill and drop it quietly. Make it forward-facing: 'next time, jump to the ball' lands completely differently to 'you keep losing your man', even though it's the same fix. Deposit before you withdraw: catch him doing something right early in the session, genuinely and specifically, so your voice isn't only the sound of bad news. And here's the move that works wonders — just ask him, one-on-one: 'how do you like getting feedback?' A thirteen-year-old who gets asked that question by his coach runs through walls for that coach. You're not lowering the bar; you're building him a way over it.
